text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

N.H. v. K.H.
,

2010 BCSC 1457

Date: 20101019

Docket:
070392

Registry: Victoria

Between:

N.H.

Claimant

And

K.H.

Respondent

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Wedge

Reasons for Judgment

Appearing on her own behalf:

N.H.

Appearing on his own behalf:

K.H.

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

September 30, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

October 19, 2010

1.
Introduction

[
1
]

The parties, N.H. and K.H., are the divorced
parents of two young boys, E.H. and C.H. The boys are five and three years of
age. Until recently, the parties lived in reasonably close proximity in the
Greater Victoria area in compliance with an order (the “Consent Order”) giving
them joint custody of the boys.

[
2
]

The boys are primarily resident with their
mother. The Consent Order provides that on a 14-day rotation, the boys live
nine days with their mother and five days with their father. Both parents are
required, as a term of the Consent Order, to reside within the Greater Victoria
area. Neither parent is permitted to relocate the children without a further
court order or consent of the other parent.

[
3
]

K.H. has now applied
for sole custody of the children. His application was precipitated by the
surreptitious relocation of the children by their mother to an undisclosed
location in Coquitlam, B.C., in early August 2010.

[
4
]

On August 17, 2010,
Macaulay J. issued an order that the children be returned to Greater Victoria.
With the assistance of police, the children were returned.

[
5
]

On August 31, 2010, the
parties appeared in chambers before R.D. Wilson J., who adjourned the
application of K.H. to a one-day hearing on September 30. The chambers judge
also ordered that K.H. and N.H. have alternating weekly access in the interim,
with K.H. bearing sole responsibility for transporting the boys between
Victoria and the Lower Mainland each week.

[
6
]

The hearing proceeded
before me on September 30. Although the chambers judge had ordered that N.H.
file her materials in advance of the hearing, N.H. did not do so. She presented
some unsworn, unfiled materials on September 30. Although she had not filed a
cross-application, N.H. advised the court that she was seeking sole custody of
the boys.

[
7
]

Both parties, who were
self-represented, advised the court that they wished to proceed with the
applications despite the shortcomings in the materials.

[
8
]

It was apparent that
the applications ought to be heard without further delay. The current parenting
arrangements are unworkable, not the least because of the high level of conflict
between the parents and the difficulties posed by the transporting of these
young children between Victoria and Vancouver in order to transfer access from
one parent to the other.

[
9
]

It was also apparent
that the court was unlikely to receive any further materials to assist in
determining the best interests of the children. Accordingly, I directed that
the matter proceed by having both parties give sworn evidence from the witness
box. I also directed that N.H. swear and file her affidavit materials, which she
did the following day.

[
10
]

I have considered the
viva
voce
evidence of the parties given in the course of the one-day hearing, as
well as the filed materials, when determining this difficult case.

2.
Issues

[
11
]

The central issue is the appropriate custody and
guardianship arrangements for these two young boys. While the parties have
joint custody of the children, the issue of mobility arises because the
children have been primarily resident with N.H. and she has now relocated to
Coquitlam.

[
12
]

The issue is not whether
the relocation of the mother (N.H.), will impair the custodial or access rights
of the father (K.H.). The issue is whether the relocation of N.H. with the
children will impair the best interests of these two young boys.

[
13
]

The relocation of N.H.,
and the circumstances surrounding it, has brought sharply into focus the issue
of whether the current custodial arrangements are in the best interests of the
children. I have concluded they are not.

[
14
]

For the reasons that
follow, I have concluded that K.H. will have sole custody of the children. It
follows that the children will reside primarily with K.H., and N.H. will have
as generous and substantial access as the circumstances allow. I will not
determine the access schedule until the parties have had the opportunity to
review and consider these reasons.

[
15
]

As these reasons will
disclose, I have concluded that N.H.’s move to Coquitlam was motivated
primarily by her desire to limit the children’s contact with their father.
Should N.H. decide to return to the Greater Victoria area, the access regime
will obviously differ from one based on her residency in Coquitlam.

[
16
]

The parties will
continue to have joint guardianship of the boys.

3.
Facts

Background:  K.H.

[
17
]

K.H. is 47 years of age. He was born in
Shellbrook, Saskatchewan. He is the middle of eleven children. His parents were
missionaries in Pakistan. His mother, who is a physician, was a medical
missionary. His father was a Lutheran pastor. The family moved to Saskatchewan
shortly before K.H. was born. They then moved to Edmonton, Alberta.

[
18
]

K.H. completed high
school in Alberta, which included a three-year commercial art program. He then
apprenticed to a commercial artist for a further two years. Thereafter, he
attended a community college in Olds, Alberta, graduating from a program known
as the Farm and Ranch Management program. He has worked in a variety of jobs,
such as occupational therapy woodworker at a hospital in Ponoka, Alberta. He
has also worked in the graphic arts business. He has worked in set design
and other areas engaging his talents and training in graphic arts. He also
purchased and operated his father’s farm in Alberta.

[
19
]

K.H. was previously
married. He has three children from that marriage, ranging in age from 21 to
26. He has a good relationship with all three children. Two of the children are
close to completing university degrees; one child has already graduated from
university and is pursuing a career in personal training.

[
20
]

K.H. has now remarried.
His spouse, T.H., also has grown children from a previous marriage with whom
she continues to have close contact.

Background:  N.H.

[
21
]

N.H. is 45 years of age. She was born in
Kinshasa, Republic of Congo. She is the second of six children. Her father was
involved in political struggle in the Congo. Some of her family members,
including N.H., moved to Canada in 1984, when N.H. was 15 years of age. Shortly
thereafter, N.H. moved to Tallahassee, Florida. N.H. gave birth to a daughter
in 1986.

[
22
]

N.H. graduated from
high school and completed several years of community college, studying
bookkeeping and accounting. Although she did not obtain a degree, she has
extensive education and work experience as a bookkeeper.

[
23
]

N.H. was previously
married in 1998. She and her former spouse bought and operated a successful
automobile/driver’s licensing registry business in Cochrane, Alberta, for
several years. N.H. was responsible, among other things, for the company’s
accounting.

[
24
]

N.H. is also a
certified fitness instructor, and has worked in the fitness industry.

The relationship between K.H. and N.H.

[
25
]

K.H. and N.H. met in 2000 when K.H. was a
customer of N.H.’s registry business. They began an extramarital
relationship. When each of their marriages failed, they continued their
relationship. They married in February 2005.

[
26
]

From the perspective of
both K.H. and N.H., the relationship was fraught with difficulties before they
married. The difficulties continued after the marriage.

[
27
]

The eldest child, E.H.,
was born in May 2005.

[
28
]

The couple bought a
property in Pritchard, B.C., that had been operated as a ranch and bed and
breakfast. They moved to the property in December 2005. K.H. was happy with
their new home but N.H. was not. She felt isolated on the ranch. From her
perspective, K.H. spent all of his time working on the ranch while she cared
for the baby. She felt he was not interested in being a parent.

[
29
]

In the fall of 2006,
after numerous disagreements, N.H. left for Victoria to visit friends. When she
returned, K.H. looked into purchasing a business for her in nearby Sorrento,
B.C., so that she could work outside the home. They put a deposit on a beauty
salon/spa in Sorrento. However, despite both their efforts, the relationship
continued to deteriorate.

[
30
]

In December 2006, N.H.
left the relationship. She decided that she wanted to live in Victoria, and
took E.H. with her.

[
31
]

K.H. travelled to
Victoria several times in early 2007, with N.H.’s encouragement, in an attempt
to reconcile. N.H. was living in an apartment in Oak Bay. Their second child,
C.H., was born in July 2007. Following the birth of C.H., K.H. assisted in
moving N.H. and the children from the apartment to a rented house. Ongoing
efforts to reconcile were unsuccessful.

[
32
]

The parties agreed to
sell the Pritchard, B.C. property. It sold for a profit, and the funds were
placed in a solicitor’s trust account pending agreement of the parties as to
their division. The funds were subsequently divided by agreement.

[
33
]

K.H. had moved back to
Alberta after the parties separated and found work there. N.H. moved to Langford,
B.C., just outside Victoria, with the children.

[
34
]

In October 2007, N.H.
decided to travel to Florida for a few weeks, where she has a support system of
friends and family. K.H. consented to N.H.’s travel plans, and provided written
consent for the children to travel with her to Miami in November 2007.

[
35
]

N.H. returned to
Langford in late December 2007. She had decided to move to the Miami area
permanently, but did not discuss her plans with K.H. Using the same written
consent provided by K.H. for the trip in November 2007, N.H. obtained entry
with the children to the United States in January 2008. She invested in a
business venture in the Miami area in order to establish herself there and
obtain visas for her children. She then set about applying for custody of the
children on the basis of her move to Miami.

[
36
]

N.H. did not disclose
her whereabouts to K.H. It was not until February 2008 that K.H. discovered
N.H. had left the Victoria area and was attempting to relocate permanently to
Miami with the children. He retained legal counsel in Alberta and commenced
proceedings to have the children returned to Alberta. He also applied for
custody of the children.

[
37
]

As a result of the
proceedings initiated by K.H., N.H. had little choice but to return to Alberta.
She did so in July 2008. In preparation for trial, examinations for discovery
were conducted. A custody and access report of a registered psychologist was
obtained. In his report, the psychologist noted the following concerning N.H.’s
relocation to Miami with the children:

[N.H.’s] moving
away without seeking [K.H.’s] consent either constitutes a poor awareness of
the children’s needs, or wilful blindness of such. Her reasons for moving
include the weather, the fact that her friends know of her affairs and divorce,
a desire to keep her distance from [K.H.], and a belief that he was not
interested in being a parent. She now states that she is very happy that [K.H.]
is making a connection [with] the children, so it is difficult to know her true
motivation.

[
38
]

Shortly before the trial was to commence, the
parties concluded the Consent Order. I have summarized the relevant terms as
follows:

o

The parties are to share joint custody of the
children;

o

The parties shall participate equally in the
educational, health care, religious and recreational decision-making for the
children;

o

The parties are to share parenting of the
children;

o

N.H. will live in the Greater Victoria area, and
the children will reside primarily with her;

o

K.H. will relocate to the Greater Victoria area
by July 2009 in order to share parenting;

o

Neither party shall relocate the children
outside of the Greater Victoria area without a court order or the written
consent of the other party;

o

N.H. shall have the children in her care for
nine days out of 14, and K.H. shall have the children in his care for five days
out of 14, on a 14‑day rotating schedule;

o

N.H. shall have custody of the children’s
passports; should K.H. elect to travel with the children outside of Canada,
N.H. shall furnish K.H. with the children’s passports at least one week prior
to the scheduled departure date;

o

Each party shall have a first right of refusal
on those occasions when the party having care of the children requires
childcare for more than four consecutive hours at a time.

[
39
]

The Consent Order also contains detailed
provisions concerning holidays (i.e. shared access during Christmas, Easter,
etc.), summer vacation, travel outside Canada, telephone contact, parenting
courses, the provision of a parenting coordinator to arbitrate disagreements
concerning education, religion, healthcare, holidays, recreation, enrolment in
curricular and extracurricular activities, travel, moves within the Greater
Victoria area, and other related issues. In other words, the Consent Order
attempted to address every potential issue that could arise from the shared
parenting of the children in the Greater Victoria area.

[
40
]

K.H. testified that the parties agreed, after
much discussion, that they would both live in the Greater Victoria area in
order to facilitate joint custody and shared parenting of the children. N.H.
had maintained a residence in the Langford area, where she was living before
she took the children to Miami, and expressed an intention to return there.
K.H. had recently remarried; he and his spouse, T.H., had a home and jobs in
Alberta, but agreed to relocate to Vancouver Island to facilitate joint
custody.

[
41
]

The agreement of the parties to live in the
Greater Victoria area formed the basis for the Consent Order and, in
particular, the shared parenting arrangements.

[
42
]

The Consent Order was issued by Madam Justice
Kent of the Alberta Queen’s Bench on October 27, 2008. It was entered as an
order of this court the following year.

[
43
]

N.H. was unemployed at the time of the Consent
Order. She was receiving approximately $6,000 per month in spousal support from
her former spouse. She maintained herself and the children on those payments,
as well as the funds from the sale of the Pritchard, B.C. property and other
payments she received from K.H.

[
44
]

The separation agreement entered into by N.H.
and her former spouse provides that N.H. is to continue receiving the $6,000
per month spousal support until December 2010.

[
45
]

Under the Consent Order, K.H. was to relocate to
the Greater Victoria area by July 2009. In the interim, he was to have access
to the children in N.H.’s home every second weekend. A term of the order was
that N.H. vacate her house on those occasions to facilitate access to the
children by K.H. and his spouse. The intention was to minimize disruption for
the children and help reduce the cost to K.H., who was paying for the travel
between Calgary and the Greater Victoria area.

[
46
]

However, when K.H. and
his spouse attempted to exercise access in accordance with the Consent Order,
N.H. refused to allow them to stay in her home. Other attempts by K.H. to
exercise access were unsuccessful. Accordingly, K.H. decided to find a place to
live in the Greater Victoria area as soon as possible.

[
47
]

K.H. and his spouse found an affordable home in
Malahat (north of Victoria) and purchased it together. They moved into the home
in April 2009. They chose the Malahat area because, while it was not strictly
speaking within the Greater Victoria area, it was proximate to Langford, where
N.H. had been renting a house before she moved to Miami.

[
48
]

K.H.’s spouse, a fitness instructor/personal
trainer by profession, found full-time work within reasonable commuting
distance from Malahat. K.H. performed small renovation jobs and freelance
commercial art work, but in his first year in Malahat he lived primarily off
the funds remaining from his share of the proceeds of the sale of the
Pritchard, B.C. property. He and his spouse had purchased the home outright,
and were able to keep their living expenses to a minimum. K.H. testified that
his focus in that first year was to establish a home for his sons and spend as
much time with them as possible.

[
49
]

Shortly after K.H. moved to Malahat, N.H. moved
to Saanich. A few months later, she moved to Sydney, B.C.

[
50
]

From April 2009 to June 2010, K.H. exercised his
access to the children for five days every two weeks, and longer periods during
holidays and vacations. The boys have their own room, toys, clothing and other
belongings permanently at the Malahat home.

[
51
]

With the exception of
two periods in January and February of 2010 when K.H. returned to Calgary to
work for three week stretches, the parties maintained the access schedule under
the Consent Order   However, the shared parenting was marred by conflict. There
were physical altercations during the transfers of access. The police were
called on more than one occasion.

[
52
]

In May 2010, N.H. moved
from Sydney to North Saanich, where she rented a house.

[
53
]

In May 2010, the
parties attended a Judicial Case Conference in Victoria before Master Bouck. The
access schedule stipulated in the Consent Order was varied by an order dated
May 31, 2010, to permit the parties to have extended and approximately equal
access to the children during July and August. The July 2010 schedule commenced
June 27, and was as follows: N.H. was to have the children from June 27 to July
10, and K.H. was to have them from July 10 to July 18; N.H. was to have access
from July 18 to July 24, and K.H. was to have access from July 24 to July 31.

[
54
]

The parties complied
with the July access schedule.

[
55
]

The August 2010 access schedule pursuant to the
order of Master Bouck contemplated the following regime:  N.H. was to have
access from August 1 to August 13, and K.H. was to have access from August 13
to August 23; N.H. was to have the children from August 23 to August 28.

[
56
]

During the summer, N.H.
had encountered difficulties with her landlord in North Saanich because she
defaulted on her monthly rental payments from time to time. Matters came to a
head in July, when she paid only $200 toward the rent. She received an eviction
notice on July 31, effective August 9. N.H. did not tell K.H. about this turn
of events.

[
57
]

The evidence is unclear on the precise timing,
but at some point in July (and perhaps earlier), N.H. decided to leave the
Greater Victoria area for the Lower Mainland. On July 28, 2010, before
receiving the eviction notice, N.H. attended a job interview at a women’s
clothing store in Burnaby. On July 30, she was offered a clerking job which was
to commence August 3, 2010. She was employed to work five days per week, eight
hours per day, at an hourly rate of $11.

[
58
]

N.H. looked for
accommodation in the area, and found a rental property she liked in Coquitlam.
She called the owner and expressed interest in renting the house immediately.

[
59
]

The children were with
K.H. at the time, in accordance with the summer access schedule. N.H. picked up
the children on the afternoon of July 31. However, she emailed K.H. the
following morning and told him she had an emergency such that K.H. would have to
take the children that day and keep them until August 6. K.H. was scheduled to
work, but changed his schedule to accommodate the request.

[
60
]

On August 2, the owner
of the Coquitlam property called N.H. and offered to rent the property to her.
On August 6, K.H. returned the children to N.H. On August 7, N.H. moved the
children and some of her belongings to Coquitlam. She left much of her
furniture in the North Saanich house and did not pay the arrears on her rent.

[
61
]

K.H. did not discover
that N.H. had moved, and taken the children with her, until August 11 when he
called her cell phone. K.H. was scheduled to take the children on vacation with
him on August 13, and required their passports to travel to the United States.
Under the Consent Order, N.H. had possession of the passports. She was to
provide them to K.H. upon his request a week in advance of travel. N.H. refused
to provide the passports to K.H. or allow the children to travel with him. She
did not disclose her Coquitlam address.

[
62
]

K.H. immediately filed
an
ex parte
application in the Victoria Registry for sole custody of the
children. He appeared before Gaul J. of this court on August 12. Gaul J.
issued an order prohibiting the removal of the children from British Columbia,
and adjourned the balance of the application to August 17, 2010. N.H. was to be
provided notice of the August 17 hearing and all of the materials on which K.H.
was relying.

[
63
]

K.H. did provide N.H.
with notice of the August 17 hearing in Victoria through email and cell phone
messages. He could not serve her with notice any other way because he did not
know where she was living.

[
64
]

N.H. responded to K.H.
by email on the morning of August 16. She advised K.H. that she did not intend
to come to Victoria to appear on the application. Her email stated, in part,
the following:

My next day off is on the 22[nd]. It will be
better for [E.H. and C.H.] if you [cooperate] with me and come up with some
schedule which doesn’t require too many traveling time. Keeping the boys
welfare in the hands of the court system isn’t a priority. I’m the boys mother
and my first duty is such.

The boys are facing many changes, the fact
that I’m working F/T as well as a new home and new school. The last thing the
boys need is more drama and devious behaviour from their parents. We are the
adults here and need to behave such as (sic).

...

You have force[d] me with your past actions
to keep my location unknown to you!   I can tell you that I’m about 20 min.
from your sister’s place in Surrey.

School starts on Sept 7, perhaps you can let
me know by phone when you want to see the boys. Days off on the 22 and 28. It
will be better if you come here and check their school.

Again I’m n[o]
longer open [to] any of your emails or your partner. It cause[s] me too much
distress.

[
65
]

K.H. appeared before Macaulay J. on August 17.
N.H. did not appear. Macaulay J. reviewed the materials, including the August
16 email of N.H., reproduced above. Macaulay J. issued an order containing a
police assist clause for the return of the children to the Greater Victoria
area in compliance with the Consent Order and the order of Master Bouck. With
the assistance of N.H.’s former landlord, K.H. obtained her address in
Coquitlam. K.H. then travelled to Coquitlam and met with two officers from the
Coquitlam RCMP detachment. They all attended at the Coquitlam home of N.H., who
was at work at the time. The children were with a babysitter. Upon reviewing
the documentation, the babysitter permitted the children to leave with K.H.,
and gave him the children’s passports.

[
66
]

Macaulay J. adjourned
the balance of the application with liberty to K.H. to bring those matters back
on with seven days notice to N.H. K.H. obtained the date of August 31, 2010 to
hear his application for sole custody of the children, and gave N.H. the requisite
notice. K.H. also advised N.H. that she was required to file any responding
materials two days before the hearing date.

[
67
]

N.H. did not file any
responding materials.

[
68
]

On August 23, K.H.
again appeared before Macaulay J., seeking to keep the children in his custody
until his application was heard and asking that the passports not be returned
to N.H. Macaulay J. directed that the passports remain with the court, but also
ordered that N.H. be permitted to exercise her scheduled access.

[
69
]

The parties appeared
before R.D. Wilson J. on August 31, 2010. N.H. sought a two-month adjournment
of the application. Instead, R.D. Wilson J. granted a 30-day adjournment,
resetting the matter for September 30. R.D. Wilson J. ordered that the parties
have interim alternating seven-day access to the children. Having been advised
by N.H. that she worked on Saturdays (which was not entirely accurate), R.D.
Wilson J. also ordered that K.H. bear the responsibility of travelling with the
children each Saturday. The return trip takes K.H. most of the day.

Evidence of K.H. concerning his move from Calgary to
Vancouver Island

[
70
]

K.H. testified that he and N.H. came to an
agreement, which formed the basis of the Consent Order, that they would live in
reasonable proximity in order to share custody and parenting of their two
children. After much discussion, they agreed on the Greater Victoria area
because N.H. had been living in Langford with the children at the time.

[
71
]

K.H. testified that he
and his spouse, with whom he has had a relationship for over three years,
agreed to relocate from Calgary where they were both gainfully employed and had
made their home, in order to make the joint custodial arrangements work. They
both experienced a reduction in their incomes in order to relocate.

[
72
]

K.H. has now obtained a
part-time position at Shawnigan Lake School, a private school close to his
home. He teaches computer graphics every Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 3:00
p.m. to 6:00 p.m. He is optimistic that his teaching hours will be extended now
that he has his “foot in the door”. With his current teaching schedule, he is
available to care for the children most of the time. The home is located on
one-third of an acre and is within walking distance of the ocean at Mill Bay.

[
73
]

As a member of the
teaching faculty of Shawnigan Lake School, K.H. is entitled to enrol his
five-year-old son, E.H., in the “Discovery School” kindergarten program offered
by the school. E.H. is registered in the program and has attended during the
weeks that he is in K.H.’s custody. Three-year-old C.H. is enrolled in a
pre-school program three mornings per week which is a few minutes’ drive from
the family home.

[
74
]

K.H.’s spouse, T.H., is
a fitness instructor/personal trainer. She gave evidence at the hearing about
the employment opportunities for fitness instructors on Vancouver Island. T.H.
found full-time work very quickly as a personal trainer for a fitness franchise
that has ten locations in the Victoria/Nanaimo area. She testified that many
fitness companies are looking for fitness instructors, and employees to perform
other work, in various locations on Vancouver Island. The starting wage is $20
per hour, and many fitness instructors/personal trainers earn $35 to 40 per
hour once they have some experience.

[
75
]

K.H. and T.H. both
testified that they want to do their best to ensure that N.H., as the
children’s mother, remains a central part of the children’s lives. They have
proposed that the boys spend from Friday to Sunday morning with their mother as
frequently as N.H. can travel to the Greater Victoria area, and/or as
frequently as the boys can reasonably make the trip to the Lower Mainland.

[
76
]

T.H. testified that she
would gladly assist N.H. to find work as a fitness instructor in the Greater
Victoria area.

The evidence of N.H. concerning her relocation to
Coquitlam

[
77
]

N.H. has significant education and experience in
bookkeeping/accounting, but testified that she could not find any work in the
Greater Victoria area as a bookkeeper. She is a certified fitness instructor,
and said she found some work at a recreation centre in the area teaching a few
dancing/fitness classes, but not enough hours to support herself. She also
testified that she had been unable to find a single job as a retail clerk in
the Greater Victoria area. She could not explain why that was the case when
numerous retail stores in the area have been advertising for retail clerk
positions.

[
78
]

As noted earlier,
N.H.’s current position is as a retail clerk in a clothing store in Metrotown
in Burnaby. She earns $11 per hour. Including her commute time, N.H. is away
from the home approximately 9 hours per day, five days per week. Her starting
and finishing times vary, as do the days of the week that she works. She pays a
babysitter $9 per hour to look after her children for 9 hours each day that she
works. She is paying $1,400 per month to rent the main floor of a two-bedroom
house in Coquitlam.

[
79
]

When asked how she was
managing to support herself on her current wage, particularly in light of the
child care costs, she said her former spouse (who continues to reside in
Calgary) is “helping her out”.

[
80
]

N.H. testified that the
$6,000 per month that she has been receiving in child support ended in December
2009. However, the separation agreement provides that the payments are to
continue until December 2010.

[
81
]

The materials also
disclosed that N.H. invested substantial funds in a business in Miami in 2008
when she attempted to move the children there. She did not provide any evidence
to the court as to the status of that business or any investments she may
continue to have in Miami.

[
82
]

N.H. has no family,
support system or ties of any nature in Coquitlam or anywhere else in the Lower
Mainland. She said she chose to move to Coquitlam, rather than anywhere else in
the Lower Mainland, because it was close to the work she obtained at Metrotown.

[
83
]

Although she moved to
Coquitlam to obtain the retail job, N.H. testified that she is about to give
her notice at the store because she now realizes the hours are too onerous and
she is not happy leaving her children with a babysitter for such long periods
of time. Instead, she has secured full-time employment working night shifts
(10:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.) at a Tim Hortons coffee shop at a wage rate of $10.50
per hour. She said she plans to work nights while her children are sleeping so
that she can be with them during the day. However, she acknowledged that she
must still pay a babysitter to be with the children during the night.

[
84
]

N.H. is of African
heritage. E.H. and C.H. are children of mixed-race. N.H. did not suggest that
she relocated the children for any reason connected to their African heritage,
although she did say that she thought the Lower Mainland had more cultural
diversity and would provide her children with a greater opportunity to
socialize with children of colour. N.H. also said her mother was Jewish, and
she hoped to raise the children in the Jewish faith. She did not suggest that
there were no opportunities to do so in the Greater Victoria area.

[
85
]

N.H. said the main
reason for her relocation to Coquitlam was to enable her to “move on with her
life”. She said that, in hindsight and in light of the Consent Order currently
governing the parties, it may have been wiser to apply to vary the terms of the
Order which prohibited her from removing the children from the Greater Victoria
area.

[
86
]

N.H.’s job at Tim
Hortons will rotate through the week, which means she will not always have
weekends off. She proposed that K.H. occasionally travel to Coquitlam to see
the boys. She said she thought that from time to time the boys could also
travel with K.H. to his home. N.H. acknowledged that once E.H. is in Grade One
next September, there will be much less flexibility with his schedule insofar
as visiting his father is concerned.

[
87
]

When asked about the
current arrangement of alternating weekly access, N.H. said it was not working.
In her words, “It is as though the children lead completely different lives
from week to week.”

[
88
]

Both N.H. and K.H.
testified that the children seem confused, anxious and stressed by the current
access arrangement.

4.
Decision

Legal principles concerning custody in the context of a
mobility issue

[
89
]

In the decision of
Falvai v. Falvai
,
2008
BCCA 503
, Madam Justice Daphne Smith, writing for the Court, discussed the
distinction between an application to vary an existing custody order and an
initial application involving a mobility issue. She said the following at
para. 21:

The only test
on a custody application is the best interests of the child. When the
application is to vary an existing custody order, the applicant must establish
that a material change of circumstances has occurred before the court will
engage in the best interest analysis. In the context of a variation
application, considerable weight, or “great respect”, is given to the custodial
parent’s views for wanting to move with a child.

[
90
]

Smith J.A., citing the well-known decision of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Gordon v. Goertz,

1996 CanLII 191 (SCC)
, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, set
out the approach to be taken on a variation application of a pre-existing
custody order (at para. 23):

1.         The parent applying for a change in the custody or access
order must meet the threshold requirement of demonstrating a material change in
the circumstances affecting the child.

2.         If the threshold is met, the judge on the application
must embark on a fresh inquiry into what is in the best interests of the child,
having regard to all the relevant circumstances relating to the child’s needs
and the ability of the respective parents to satisfy them.

3.         This inquiry is based on the findings of the judge who
made the previous order and evidence of the new circumstances.

4.         The inquiry does not begin with a legal presumption in
favour of the custodial parent, although the custodial parent’s views are
entitled to great respect.

5.         Each case turns on its own unique circumstances. The only
issue is the best interest of the child in the particular circumstances of the
case.

6.         The focus is on the best interest of the child, not the
interests and rights of the parents.

7.         More particularly, the judge should consider,
inter
alia
:

(a)        the existing custody arrangement and relationship between
the child and the custodial parent;

(b)        the existing access arrangement and the relationship
between the child and the access parent;

(c)        the desirability of maximizing contact between the child
and both parents;

(d)        the views of the child;

(e)        the custodial parent’s reason for moving,
only

where in the exceptional case where it is relevant to that parent’s ability to
meet the needs of the child;

(f)         disruption to the child of a change in custody;

(g)        disruption to the child consequent on removal from
family, schools, and the community he or she has come to know.

[Emphasis in
original]

[
91
]

In the recent decision of our Court of Appeal in

S.S.L. v. J.W.W.
,

2010 BCCA 55
,
Huddart J.A., writing for the
Court, stated at para. 24 that the court’s task in cases such as this—where
one parent wishes to relocate to another city—is to analyze the evidence in the
context of four possible alternatives: (i) primary residence with the mother;
(ii) primary residence with the father; (iii) shared parenting in the mother’s
chosen place of residence; (iv) shared parenting in the father’s chosen place
of residence. However, the court’s first task is to determine which parent is
to have primary residence. Where the question of primary residence is evenly
balanced and the court finds that the best interests of the children require
both parents to be in the same area, the court must then choose between the
shared parenting options proposed by each parent without presuming that the
current regime is the preferred one.

Application of the law to the present case

[
92
]

This case poses unique challenges because the
mother has already relocated with the children, and has done so in breach of a
court order.

[
93
]

The circumstances of this case differ slightly
from those in most mobility cases in other respects. This is clearly a
variation application, but the parties are bound by a Consent Order, not an
order issued after a trial on the basis of reasons by a trial judge. Pursuant
to the Consent Order, both parents have agreed to be bound by geographic
limitations as a condition of the joint custody arrangement. Further, neither
parent is the custodial parent. The parents are joint custodians of the
children under the Consent Order.

[
94
]

Under the Consent Order, the children are
primarily resident with their mother. From the time the parties first separated
in December 2006, until N.H. returned from Miami in July 2008, the children
were primarily in the care of N.H. That is because K.H. was resident and
working in Alberta, and N.H. had chosen to live in Langford, B.C., during most
of 2007. For the first six months of 2008, N.H. had the children in Miami
without K.H.’s consent.

[
95
]

However, since July 2008, the children have been
in the day-to-day care of their father for substantial amounts of time. They
have had a home with their father since April 2009. Although they are with K.H.
only slightly more than one-third of the time, there is stability and routine
in their lives during that time. They have their own permanent space in the
home. K.H. sees to the ongoing daily needs of the children when they are with
him and his spouse. They attend the family church. They participate in sports
programs. K.H. is entitled by the terms of the Consent Order to be as involved
as the mother in all of the significant decisions affecting the children’s
lives, and he has made every effort to exercise his right to be so involved.

[
96
]

There has clearly been
a material change in the circumstances affecting the children. N.H. has
unilaterally relocated the children to the Lower Mainland in contravention of
the Consent Order. The shared parenting arrangements, on which the Consent
Order was entirely based, are no longer workable.

[
97
]

I am mindful that in
custody matters the court must give considerable weight to the objective of
maximizing contact between the children and both parents. However, as in most
cases involving mobility, that objective necessarily gives way to other
considerations.

[
98
]

There is no prior decision
of a trial judge. Any “fresh inquiry” is limited to consideration of the
arrangements to which the parties agreed in the Consent Order.

[
99
]

There is no collateral
evidence concerning the parenting abilities of each parent or the attachment of
the children to each parent. There is no Section 15 Custody/Access Report.

[
100
]

Neither parent is the custodial parent,
although the primary residence of the children was with N.H.

[
101
]

The ages of the children are such that it
would not be appropriate for the court to obtain their views.

[
102
]

As has been emphasized in many recent
judgments concerning the mobility rights of parents, the trial judge should
consider the reasons underlying the decision of the custodial parent to
relocate
only
if they are relevant to that parent’s ability to meet the
needs of the child.

[
103
]

I have concluded that N.H.’s motive for
relocating to Coquitlam
is
relevant to her ability to parent E.H. and
C.H.

[
104
]

N.H. has no ties to the Lower Mainland. She has no family or friends
there. There is no apparent reason for her decision to relocate. I do not
accept her assertion that she moved for economic reasons. First, I do not
accept that N.H. could not secure work in the Greater Victoria area, given her
education, training and experience. She once ran a very successful
business. She has bookkeeping and accounting training and experience. She
is a certified fitness instructor, and I accept the evidence of T.H. that there
are abundant opportunities in the Greater Victoria area for fitness
instructors. There are also retail clerking jobs in the Greater Victoria area
comparable to the one N.H. took in Burnaby and now, less than two months later,
is leaving. At the very least, in the Greater Victoria area there is a
multitude of jobs available at coffee shops such as the one N.H. has now
accepted at Tim Hortons.

[
105
]

Second, N.H. was aware before accepting the
job at Metrotown that it would pay very little more than she would be required
to pay for a babysitter to look after her children. In that regard, at least,
the move made no economic sense. N.H. was capable of earning more as an
occasional fitness instructor (work that she had obtained in the Greater
Victoria area just before she moved to Coquitlam) than working full-time as a
retail clerk at $11 per hour and paying a babysitter $9 per hour.

[
106
]

N.H. knew that she was required under the
Consent Order to give K.H. the right of first refusal to care for the children
in the event she required childcare for more than four hours. She knew that
K.H. had the flexibility in his schedule to provide much of that care,
particularly on weekends. Had she obtained work in the Greater Victoria area,
N.H. would have had to give K.H. the opportunity to care for the children while
she was at work. Not only would it have made economic sense to do so, but it
would have provided the children more time with their father.

[
107
]

Perhaps most telling is the fact that N.H.
did not provide the court with any cogent reason for moving the children in the
absence of their father’s consent and to an undisclosed location.

[
108
]

In the face of this evidence, it is
difficult to conclude that N.H. had any motive for the relocation other than to
limit the children’s contact with their father. Such an improper motive is
relevant because it impacts negatively on the court’s assessment of N.H.’s
parenting abilities and, in particular, her ability to parent cooperatively
with the children’s father.

[
109
]

Further, N.H.’s surreptitious relocation of
the children, in the face of the Consent Order, is evidence of a troubling
indifference not only to her responsibilities as a parent who shares custody
jointly with the children’s father, but to compliance with orders of the court
which govern her custodial relationship with the children. The email she sent
to K.H. on the eve of the August 17 appearance before Macaulay J. evinces
complete disregard for the terms of the Consent Order and the judicial process
generally.

[
110
]

Even more troubling is the fact that this
is not the first time N.H. has covertly attempted to relocate the children. She
was aware of the comments of the psychologist reporting to the court in 2008,
who observed that her attempts to relocate the children at that time without
K.H.’s consent reflected a disregard, or wilful blindness, concerning the needs
of the children.

[
111
]

N.H.’s August 16 email is telling in
another respect. She wrote: “The boys are facing many changes, the fact that
I’m working F/T as well as a new home and new school. The last thing the boys
need is more drama and devious behaviour from their parents. We are the adults
here and need to behave [as such].”  The children are indeed facing the many
changes referenced by N.H. Unfortunately, N.H. does not understand that the
devious behaviour is hers, and the disruption in the boys’ lives has been
caused by her precipitous and ill-advised move to Coquitlam.

[
112
]

Both parents are adamant that joint custody
is unworkable. Both say the boys are suffering from the current arrangement.
Their views are not determinative, of course, but in this case I am satisfied
they are accurate.

[
113
]

As the case law indicates, the court’s
first task is to determine the best interests of the children, having regard to
the relevant circumstances relating to their needs, and the ability of the
respective parents to satisfy those needs.

[
114
]

It is clear that K.H. and N.H. both love
their children. However, the actions of N.H. reflect her inability to share
custody of the children at this time.

[
115
]

After concluding that joint custody is no
longer an option, I went on to consider what I anticipate will be the children’s
circumstances if they move with their mother to Coquitlam, and their likely
circumstances if they stay with their father in Malahat.

[
116
]

These children are five and three years of
age. They have known very little stability in their brief lives, and both parents
agree the instability is taking a toll on them. The only stability they have
known is that which they have experienced with their father and his spouse
since they purchased their home in Malahat in the spring of 2009. The boys now
have some roots in the community. In the event they stay with their father,
there will be continuity with the friends, both adult and children, with whom
they have had ongoing contact. There are excellent schools and extracurricular
activities in close proximity to the home. E.H. will continue in the Discovery
School offered by Shawnigan Lake School. C.H. will soon be enrolled there as
well.

[
117
]

K.H. and his spouse, T.H., have made
significant efforts to make a home in Malahat. They have purchased a home and
obtained employment in the area. They did so in compliance with the Consent
Order and in an effort to make the joint custody arrangement with N.H. work.

[
118
]

There is no reasonable prospect of
stability in the boys’ lives if their primary residence remains with N.H. She
has moved them numerous times in the past two years. Beyond enrolling E.H. in a
school in Coquitlam, N.H. has no plan for the children. She has no plan for her
own future, except to move the children away from their father. She has no
roots in Coquitlam, and if history is any lesson, she will soon be moving
elsewhere.

[
119
]

Finally, for reasons already discussed,
joint custody of the children in either Greater Victoria or Coquitlam would be
neither workable nor in the best interests of the children.

5.
Conclusion

[
120
]

I have concluded that it is in the best interests of the children to
award sole custody of E.H. and C.H. to their father, K.H. N.H. will have
generous and substantial access to the children, but it must be age-appropriate
access given the distance and logistics of travel between Coquitlam and
Malahat. As I indicated at the outset of these reasons, I will remain seized of
this matter in order to deal with all matters arising from the decision,
including the schedule for access by N.H.

[
121
]

The parties will remain joint guardians of
E.H. and C.H. Joint guardianship will allow for shared decision-making by the
parents in regard to significant issues in the children’s lives, such as
medical, educational and religious decisions. The precise terms of the
guardianship order, including a mechanism should the parents not agree on those
decisions, will be settled once I hear from the parties concerning access and
any other matters arising from these reasons.

[
122
]

contact
Vancouver

on Friday, October 22, 2010, to confirm their availability to appear, either in
person or by telephone, on Thursday, October 28, 2010, in
Vancouver
, at
10:00 a.m., to make submissions concerning access schedules. Until all matters
